title: Comparative Study of Quantum and Classical Machine Learning Models in Binary Classification
abstract: A potential path forward is Quantum Machine Learning (QML), which aims to leverage quantum computing in conjunction with classical machine learning to enhance computing efficiency and the expressiveness of models. In this paper, two different quantum classifiers - Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) and Quantum Kernel Support Vector Machine (QSVM) - are compared with three classical classifiers as baseline classifiers - Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) - on the Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset. The quantum circuits were created in the PennyLane framework and simulated on a classical backend. However, in terms of accuracy, classical Logistic Regression performed better with an accuracy of 97.8%, classical SVM and QSVM with an accuracy of 95.6% each, although the Quantum VQC achieved a lower accuracy of 88.9% and had a recall of 100% for the benign class, though it correctly identified only 12 of the 17 malignant cases (a malignant-class recall of approximately 70.6%). The drawback of quantum models is the higher training time; however, since the quantum circuit needs to be classically simulated, the quantum SVM took 23.29 seconds compared to less than 0.01 seconds for the classical linear models. These results indicate that for small structured datasets, classifiers based on quantum computing have not yet surpassed well-tuned classical counterparts. In some respects (e.g., benign-class recall), they perform competitively, though not on malignant-class recall, where the VQC in particular performed worse than the classical baselines, which is worth further investigation on real quantum computers.
summary: This paper compares Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) and Quantum Kernel SVM (QSVM) against classical ML models on a diagnostic dataset. While quantum models showed some competitive performance in specific metrics, they were significantly slower to train and less accurate than classical baselines. The study concludes that quantum advantage is not yet demonstrated for small, structured datasets.
main_problem: The paper comparatively studies the performance of Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models against established classical Machine Learning (ML) models for binary classification.
main_result: On a small, structured dataset, classical models, particularly Logistic Regression, significantly outperformed the quantum classifiers in terms of overall accuracy and computational efficiency.
method: The study involved training and testing VQC and QSVM quantum models alongside classical counterparts (LR, SVM, MLP) using the Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset.
model_or_system: The quantum models utilized 4-qubit circuits simulated on a classical backend using PennyLane, featuring angle-encoding feature maps and variational ansatz layers. Classical models were trained on PCA-reduced features.
key_observables: Accuracy (best: 97.8% for LR), Recall (Malignant Class: LR/SVM/QSVM at 94.1% vs VQC at 70.6%), and Training Time (Classical: <0.01s vs QSVM: 23.29s).
important_parameters: The comparison was performed on a small, structured dataset (Breast Cancer Wisconsin) using 4 principal components.
main_assumptions: The quantum circuits were simulated entirely on a classical backend, meaning the results do not reflect performance on actual quantum hardware.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the MLP architecture, the VQC quantum circuit diagram, and comparisons of performance metrics like accuracy, recall, and training time across all five models.
paper_structure: The paper follows a comparative structure, detailing the setup (dataset, feature reduction), presenting the architectures of both quantum and classical models, and concluding with a quantitative comparison of performance metrics.
why_interesting: Although the focus is ML, the comparison highlights the current overhead and performance gap between NISQ-era quantum simulations and classical ML benchmarks, which is a key topic in quantum computation feasibility studies.
